# Education in Pakistan
Education in Pakistan is organized into several formal stages: pre-school (ages 3–5), primary (grades 1–5), middle (grades 6–8), secondary (grades 9–12), and tertiary. Primary school completion stands at 67.5%, with net attendance rates below global averages. The curriculum encompasses arts, sciences, languages, religious studies, and Pakistan Studies, with single-sex and coeducational institutions prevalent. Secondary education comprises national board exams (SSC and HSSC) and alternative qualifications like British GCE/IGCSE or AP, plus technical and vocational tracks (TSC, DAE). Tertiary education includes professional degrees (engineering, medicine, law, etc.), bachelor’s and master’s programs, and a developing teacher education system. Public spending on education is low (around 2% of GDP), resulting in poor infrastructure, especially at the primary level, and frequent calls for increased investment.
Major challenges include gender disparity, with women significantly underrepresented and facing barriers to access and decision-making, though progress has been made toward reducing inequality. Literacy stands at 60.65% (2023), with marked regional and gender gaps. Educational quality is compromised by shortages of teachers, outdated curricula, rote learning, and infrastructural neglect. Madrasas provide religious instruction, influential in areas where state schools are lacking; religious content also permeates the national curriculum. Reforms aim to address access, quality, and teacher preparation, while non-formal and distance learning modes (e.g., Teleschool, AIOU) seek to reach marginalized populations and remote areas. International education options, including a sizeable international school sector and Pakistani students studying abroad, diversify the system. Despite persistent problems, some Pakistani institutions and alumni, especially in science, engineering, and technology, have achieved international recognition.
